lede: Quadrature and cubature replace an integral by a weighted sum over a few nodes. The atlas collects the smallest known cubature rules with positive weights and nodes inside the domain, for degrees 1 to 30 (depending on the domain, up to the degree for which a rule is available) on the interval, triangle, square, tetrahedron and cube. Typical uses are the finite element method, multiple integrals and any computation where a function evaluation is expensive.

oqCube6:
Open question (cube, degree 6): is N_PI = 22 minimal, and is N_PO = 21 minimal? The proven lower bound is only dim P3 = 20.

21 nodes inside the cube: thousands of random starts found no rule. All 12 distinct 21-node rules found with positive weights (up to symmetry) have nodes outside the cube; the closest one reaches max|x| = 1.272 (the PO rule shown here).

20 nodes, anywhere: such a rule exists exactly if the moment matrix M(3) has a flat extension M(4) (Curto-Fialkow). This is a system of 75 quadratic equations in the 36 moments of degree 7. Numerically it has no real or complex solution, but no algebraic certificate of degree 4 or lower exists, so a proof needs heavier computer algebra (degree 6 or more).

For the disk, Easwaran, Fialkow and Petrovic (2006) proved the analogous 10-node case; the next case there is open as well.

notes.interval: On the interval the Gauss–Legendre rule is optimal: counting value, lower bound and Gauss product coincide, so no rule needs fewer than ⌈(n+1)/2⌉ nodes.
notes.triangle: The rules are at most 2 nodes above the counting value and never larger than the Xiao–Gimbutas rules. At degrees 3, 7, 10, 15, 17 and 18 to 20 they are smaller. The comparison is only partly fair, because the literature rules are fully symmetric.
notes.square: At the odd degrees 9 and 11 the rules reach the Möller bound (17 and 24 nodes). Compared with the smallest known fully symmetric rules (for example 57 nodes at degree 17), the centrally symmetric rules here need fewer nodes (54). From degree 21 the rules lie at most 1 node above the counting value at even degrees and below it at odd degrees.
notes.tetra: The counting value is a good forecast here: for all degrees the rules are 0 to 5 nodes above it. Degrees 19 and 20 (389 and 446 nodes) are the most recently improved; the search there is not exhausted. The fully symmetric rules in the literature are larger (degree 9: 59, degree 10: 81).
notes.cube: The cube shows the widest gap between the Gauss product and the smallest known rules: from degree 10 the product needs more than three times as many nodes. Compared with fully symmetric rules (degree 9: 58, degree 15: 199) the centrally symmetric rules here are smaller (48 and 186).

exSub: The rules integrate functions that are not polynomials. The plot shows the relative error against the exact value, over the degree. The orange line is the computing accuracy; below it the error is only rounding noise. Square root and logarithm are shifted so that they stay finite on the whole domain, the branch point lies just outside. The error spans 16 orders of magnitude and therefore needs a logarithmic scale.

srcNote: Square and triangle (degrees 21 to 30) and tetrahedron (degrees 21 to 23) come from our own search and are certified like the other rules. Where the table ends (tetrahedron from degree 24), no rule better than the Gauss product has been computed yet. ‡ Cube: fully symmetric rule (group Oh or Td), found with symmetry reduction. The certificate holds in the symmetry-reduced system (orbit parameters and orbit weights as unknowns, moments of the invariant polynomials as equations) and shows an exact symmetric rule nearby.

exNnote: Same node count with a smaller error means a better rule. Circles: the rules of this page (degrees 1 to 30), diamonds: fully symmetric rules from the literature with real nodes (square and cube Diallo–Worku, triangle Witherden–Vincent, tetrahedron Jaśkowiec–Sukumar), dashed: Gauss product. Which rule is ahead at equal node count depends on the function; the documentation explains why (section “Why does the Gauss product …”). The ringed circle is the selected degree.
exNnoteI: On the interval the Gauss product is the rule found; there is nothing to compare.
capSurf: Function surface over the domain; the columns (green: function value positive, red: negative) stand on a partition of the domain (Voronoi-like, each cell holds one node), the base area of a column equals the weight, all bases together make up the domain, the height is the function value. Dragging rotates the view.
capCloud: Cloud of sample points in the domain, coloured by function value, with the Voronoi cells of the nodes (green: function value positive, red: negative) and the nodes in dark. Dragging rotates the view.
curve: Function curve with bars: width = weight, height = function value at the node. The sum of the bar areas is the approximation of the integral.
shiftTxt: s = x₁+…+x_d + d, d = dimension (boxes);  s = x₁+…+x_d (simplices)
certH: Proof: rules lie near exact solutions
certSub: A rule whose moments are correct to 10<sup>−15</sup> is not yet an exact rule. The Newton–Kantorovich certificate checks for every rule on this page whether an exact solution of the moment equations exists near the stored numbers.

foot: This page was generated by AI: Claude (model claude-sonnet-5-5) by Anthropic produced the search, computation, checks, text and code, commissioned and directed by Jörg Kubitz. Mistakes are possible; the certificates and source code allow verification. All rules are computed numerically; the cube rules from degree 21 come from a search with symmetry reduction. Gauss–Legendre on the interval and the reference values of the examples are analytic or determined to high order.
certSumTpl: {dom}: {ok} of {tot} rules certified (h ≤ ½); for {ins} of them the ball around the rule safely stays inside the domain with positive weights. For the others at least one node lies on the domain boundary: an exact solution is guaranteed to exist, but its position inside the closed domain is only known up to the radius.
